title: Building a 2-meter J-pole antenna this weekend
summary: Copper pipe, a few fittings, and a Saturday: a classic 2-meter J-pole you can hang and check with an SWR meter.

blocks.title: A J-pole from copper pipe
blocks.body: The J-pole is a half-wave radiator with a quarter-wave matching stub. On 2 meters it is short enough to build from plumbing parts, hang from a mast, and tune with an SWR meter before you call it done.

items.label: About 5 ft of 3/4-inch copper pipe and matching tee and end caps
items.detail: Exact cut lengths depend on your velocity factor and target frequency — measure twice.

items.label: SO-239 chassis connector and short leads or hose clamps for the feed
items.detail: The feed attaches on the stub, not at the bottom of the long element.

items.label: Mast clamp or UV-stable hang point
items.detail: Keep metal mounting hardware clear of the matching region until you know your SWR.

items.label: SWR meter or antenna analyzer covering 144–148 MHz
items.detail: Building without a way to measure match is guessing.

blocks.heading: Saturday build order
items: Cut the long element near 1/2 wave and the stub near 1/4 wave for your target frequency in the 2-meter band (example starting lengths often land near 60 in and 19 in for copper — verify against a current dimension chart).
Sweat or clamp the tee so the stub parallels the long element with a small air gap.
Attach the feed on the stub side: shield toward the shorted bottom, center toward the open stub — slide for lowest SWR.
Mount it clear of metal gutters, check SWR across the band, and note the dip frequency before you weatherproof.

blocks.title: RF and height basics
blocks.body: Stay off power lines, do not transmit into an untuned antenna at high power while adjusting, and treat rooftop work like any other ladder job. A J-pole is simple; gravity and mains voltage are not.

blocks.heading: What good enough looks like
blocks.body: Aim for SWR under about 1.5:1 at your usual simplex or repeater frequency. If the dip is low in the band, shorten the radiator slightly; if it is high, lengthen or adjust the feed point. Once it is stable, tape or seal the feed connections so rain does not undo Saturday's work.
